By Timour Azhari and Jana Choukeir
RIYADH, Nov 8 (Reuters) - An administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris following an attempted attack on Sunday, with no injuries or fatalities reported, the kingdom’s Energy Ministry said.
A Reuters witness saw blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the capital’s King Abdullah Financial District.
The incident, which the ministry said caused limited damage, came after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis towards Riyadh.
Aramco was not immediately available for comment, and there was no immediate statement from the Houthis.
Multiple loud booms were heard in Riyadh earlier on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, shortly after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat in the region. Authorities later announced that the danger had passed.
The Saudi-led coalition that has been fighting the Houthis subsequently said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the kingdom’s southern region.
The Houthis have stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities since fighting resumed in July and became another front in the wider Middle East war reignited following the US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February.
Saudi Arabia has carried out airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.
ALERTS IN OIL-RICH EASTERN PROVINCE
Earlier on Sunday, Saudi Civil Defense issued and later lifted warnings in several areas of the oil-rich Eastern Province, including Dhahran, home to the headquarters of state oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Eastern Province holds most of the kingdom’s oil and gas reserves. Saudi Aramco’s headquarters suffered extensive damage in an attack in October.
An attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 10 killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Saudi authorities.
The renewed hostilities have shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that had largely halted fighting between the two sides.
Saudi Arabia led a coalition of Arab states into Yemen in 2015 to restore the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.

The technology-heavy SSE Star 50 index has plunged 40% in less than four months, wiping out at least $480 billion in market value, while losses have spread across companies linked to artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and semiconductor manufacturing. The decline has prompted Beijing to mobilise state-backed funds, insurers and regulators to support the market, highlighting growing concerns about the sustainability of China’s technology rally.
The broader exposure is significant. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related companies account for 42% of China's total stock market capitalisation, with more than 3,000 listed companies generating AI-related revenue. Their combined market value was estimated at around $10 trillion as of March.
Several prominent companies have already suffered substantial losses. Battery maker CATL has fallen 35% this year, while robot maker Unitree has lost half its value since its August initial public offering. Shares of optical component maker Suzhou TFC Communication and printed circuit board manufacturer Victory Giant Technology have dropped as much as 26% over the past week.
The selloff reflects a combination of elevated valuations, intensifying domestic competition, higher energy costs, tariffs and the possibility that the United States and Europe could restrict access to Chinese technology and data-centre equipment. However, weakening domestic demand and the prolonged property crisis are adding to investor concerns.
China's blue-chip CSI 300 index has fallen around 21% from its June peak, despite earlier stimulus measures aimed at supporting the economy and combating deflation. The country's $21.5 trillion economy remains heavily dependent on exports, while the property downturn continues to weigh on household confidence and spending.
The weakness in Chinese equities also contrasts with gains elsewhere in Asia. The CSI 300 has declined nearly 14% this year, while Taiwan's benchmark has gained 56% and South Korea's has risen 36%. Japan's Nikkei 225 has advanced more than 25%.
China's challenge is particularly significant because its AI industry has continued to produce technological breakthroughs, but investors have struggled to translate those achievements into comparable stock market gains. Unlike companies benefiting from semiconductor hardware and upstream infrastructure investments elsewhere in Asia, many of China's AI successes have centred on developing new models.
For Xi, the consequences extend beyond market valuations. Beijing wants to encourage households to invest in equities, particularly technology companies, to finance AI infrastructure development and reduce dependence on property as a store of household wealth. Property accounts for roughly 70% of Chinese household wealth, and its prolonged crisis has reinforced concerns about deflation.
However, repeated stock market collapses and regulatory interventions have damaged retail investor confidence. The Shanghai Composite remains around 4,000, well below its October 2007 peak of approximately 6,100, despite China's economy growing nearly sixfold since then.
The government's history of technology-sector crackdowns, unpredictable regulation and weak corporate governance has also made households cautious about investing in equities. Retail investors account for much of China's market turnover, leaving trading vulnerable to policy signals and speculation rather than fundamentals.
Even after the recent decline, the STAR 50 trades at around 38 times forward earnings, compared with approximately 20 times for the Nasdaq 100, suggesting valuations remain elevated.
China remains a formidable competitor in artificial intelligence, with Bloomberg Intelligence projecting that the country could lead the world in large language models by 2030. But a prolonged market downturn could undermine Beijing's efforts to use private capital markets to finance technological development.
An extended AI correction would therefore threaten not only investor wealth and China's technology ambitions but also Xi's broader plan to establish a stock-market-driven alternative to the struggling property sector.

California Representative Robert Garcia, who is in line to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee next year after Democrats’ sweeping midterm election victory, said investigations will focus on Musk’s involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency’s firing of federal workers last year, and Miller’s role in Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown.

The crackdown on immigration, which included operations in which two people were fatally shot in Minnesota by federal agents, has proven widely unpopular. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in October found that only 37% approved of Trump’s handling of immigration, down from 50% when he took office.
Voters delivered a historic rebuke to Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm election, but with Miller as White House chief of staff, the Trump administration is expected to continue its aggressive approach to immigration enforcement, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress, say officials and experts who spoke to Reuters.

title: How sustainable is the AI investment boom after Thursday’s selloff?
full_text:
Investing.com -- The artificial intelligence investment boom is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain at its current pace as technology companies pour billions of dollars into infrastructure without a corresponding acceleration in revenues, raising the risk of an eventual spending slowdown that could weigh on economic growth, Capital Economics said.
Capital Economics said it remained positive about AI's long-term potential to boost productivity but questioned whether revenues would grow quickly enough to justify the unprecedented capital expenditure. The research firm expects AI investment growth to slow in 2027 before total investment falls by around 10% in 2028, marking a shift from a major driver of economic growth to a potential drag.
The warning comes as the five largest US hyperscalers – Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle – prepare to spend a combined $800 billion on capital expenditure this year, with spending expected to reach $1 trillion or more in 2027. Much of the increase since 2023 has been driven by investments in AI infrastructure, including data centres, servers and networking equipment.
However, the revenue hurdle to justify the spending is substantial. Capital Economics estimates that annual AI-related revenues from external customers would need to reach between $1.7 trillion and $1.9 trillion by 2030, compared with an estimated $150 billion to $200 billion currently. That would require revenues to increase roughly ninefold to 12-fold within four years.
The firm identified three potential sources of revenue growth: productivity gains that allow AI providers to capture a share of additional economic output, displacement of existing software and business-services providers, and savings from reduced labour costs. However, achieving the required returns would demand much larger productivity improvements and a more significant transfer of income from workers to capital than the firm currently expects.
Physical constraints could also limit the expansion. Shortages of advanced semiconductors and electricity, alongside rising opposition to data centres over their consumption of land, power and water, could delay projects. Capital Economics said political pressure following Democrats' gains in the US midterm elections could also result in tighter planning restrictions, particularly at the state level.
The investment slowdown could have significant implications for economic growth, particularly in the United States and major Asian technology exporters. AI investment has recently added around 0.3 percentage points to annual US GDP growth, a contribution that could largely disappear next year as spending growth slows. An outright 10% decline in AI investment in 2028 could shave another 0.1 percentage point off US GDP.
Taiwan and South Korea face greater exposure because of their dependence on AI-related manufacturing and exports. Capital Economics estimates that the diminishing boost from AI demand could reduce annual real GDP growth by around three percentage points in Taiwan and one percentage point in South Korea next year, relative to recent rates. The impact could deepen in 2028, reaching 5.5 percentage points in Taiwan and 1.5 percentage points in South Korea.
The report also warned that disappointing investment returns could create financial spillovers as hyperscalers increasingly turn to external financing. While AI infrastructure spending was initially funded largely through companies' own cash flows, debt issuance, equity financing, leases and private credit have become more important. A deterioration in revenues could therefore expose lenders and other investors to losses, potentially tightening financial conditions.
Capital Economics said the risks would remain relatively contained if the investment boom turned soon, with outstanding hyperscaler bonds still amounting to about $500 billion, or roughly 6% of the $8.3 trillion US non-financial corporate bond market. However, a prolonged investment boom financed increasingly through debt could create much larger financial vulnerabilities.
Despite the risks, the firm does not expect an abrupt collapse in AI investment or a severe economic downturn. Existing infrastructure, replacement spending and continued investment should support further AI adoption, even if spending on physical infrastructure moderates. Software and applications linked to AI deployment could also prove more resilient than spending on GPUs, servers and networking equipment.
Capital Economics' central view is that the AI investment boom will eventually adjust to a more sustainable pace rather than signal the end of AI's economic potential. The greater concern, it said, is that a prolonged period of excessive investment could expose financial and economic imbalances, particularly if the productivity gains and revenues needed to justify the spending fail to materialise.

title: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
full_text:
By Jonathan Stempel
Nov 7 (Reuters) - Berkshire Hathaway has accelerated its stock repurchases, as new CEO Greg Abel demonstrated a greater willingness than his predecessor Warren Buffett to put the conglomerate’s enormous cash hoard to use.
The Omaha, Nebraska-based company also reported on Saturday lower third-quarter profit, with operating earnings down 6% to $12.71 billion and net earnings down 28% to $22.11 billion. These reflected declines in insurance businesses such as Geico, and lower gains on common stock investments.
Berkshire said it repurchased $9.6 billion of its own stock between July and September and about $2 billion more in October, in addition to $4.8 billion earlier in the year.
The quarter was the third since Abel, 64, became chief executive. Buffett, 96, had difficulty finding things to buy toward the end of his 60 years at the helm. He remains chairman emeritus, after his son Howard Buffett replaced him as chairman in September.
Following the repurchases, Berkshire ended September with $356.9 billion of cash and equivalents, down from $380.2 billion six months earlier. Its biggest year for buybacks was 2021, when it repurchased $27 billion of stock.
Berkshire owns dozens of businesses including several insurers and reinsurers, the BNSF railroad, utilities, industrial and manufacturing companies, and retail brands such as Brooks running shoes, Fruit of the Loom underwear and See’s Candies. It also owned $335.5 billion of stocks such as Alphabet, Apple and American Express as of September 30.
Many investors view the $1.21 trillion conglomerate as a barometer for the US economy.
LESS VOLATILE, HIGH QUALITY
While the economy grew at an annualized 3.4% rate in the third quarter, according to the advance estimate of the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis, elevated inflation and gas prices are dampening consumers’ ability to spend.
Berkshire said that "considerable uncertainty" remains about economic and geopolitical events, including tariffs and wars, and several retailing businesses are experiencing "sluggish" demand because of that uncertainty and its impact on consumer confidence.
Nonetheless, shares of Berkshire, which owns several businesses that benefit from higher gasoline and electricity prices, reached record highs this week despite a broader market selloff driven by investor worries about artificial intelligence and debt-fueled spending by technology companies.
Since the end of September, Berkshire’s stock has outgained the S&P 500 by more than 18 percentage points, after lagging significantly since Buffett announced in May 2025 he was stepping down as CEO. For all of 2026, Berkshire has beaten the index by more than 5 percentage points.
Cathy Seifert, a CFRA Research analyst who rates Berkshire "hold," said Berkshire’s balance sheet strength, diversification and share repurchases provide tailwinds.
"Investors may be rotating into less volatile, high-quality names such as Berkshire," Seifert said. "The question is how much investors will accept short-term shortfalls in exchange for owning a company with a strong balance sheet and which successfully transitioned to a post-Buffett era."
SUPPORT FOR AI
Berkshire’s $12.71 billion of third-quarter operating profit, or about $8,954 per Class A share, fell from $13.49 billion a year earlier. Profit from insurance declined 26%, and from underwriting fell 43%.
The $22.11 billion of net income included unrealized gains and losses on stocks that Berkshire is not selling. Berkshire urges investors to ignore the resulting volatility.
Revenue increased 11% to $105.65 billion, the second straight quarter of double-digit percentage growth, despite declines in consumer businesses such as Fruit of the Loom underwear and Forest River RVs.
Results reflected purchases this year of Occidental Petroleum’s chemicals business for $9.4 billion and the Taylor Morrison home builder for $6.8 billion.
Berkshire has also spent billions of dollars on Alphabet shares to help Google’s parent expand in AI, though the stock trades below the discounted prices that Berkshire paid. It also took a 4% stake in Italian software technology company Bending Spoons.
BNSF, ENERGY, INDUSTRIAL BUSINESSES FARE BETTER
Geico’s 45% pretax profit decline reflected a willingness to charge lower premiums, to help regain customers lost during a multiyear effort to improve underwriting quality and reduce overhead.
The insurer’s loss ratio, or percentage of premiums paid to cover claims, rose to 76.6% from 71.5% a year earlier. Claims also grew in other Berkshire insurance and reinsurance businesses.
Seifert called Geico’s results weak relative to those of Allstate and Progressive. She also said Berkshire’s limited financial disclosures, long a concern for analysts, make it harder to pinpoint problems and how to fix them.
"Limited disclosures are fine when everything goes in the right direction, but become a point of vulnerability" when they do not, she said.
Profit at BNSF rose 19%, benefiting from fuel surcharges and higher volumes of consumer, agricultural and energy products.
Profit rose 8% at Berkshire Hathaway Energy, which owns utilities, natural gas pipelines and Berkshire’s namesake real estate brokerage.
Industrial businesses fared well. In that unit, aerospace and industrial gas turbine sales helped Precision Castparts boost pretax profit by 30%.
Profit from consumer products businesses declined, mainly because of lower tax credits at Duracell, while higher gas prices boosted the Pilot truck stop chain.

title: How a digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president
full_text:
By Daniela Desantis and Brendan O’Boyle
ASUNCION, Nov 8 (Reuters) - For years, Paraguay’s digital bank, ueno, stood out as a homegrown success story, luring roughly half the country’s people to open accounts and offering many the opportunity to hold a bank account for the very first time.
But over just five days this week, the bank collapsed, freezing the savings of nearly 3 million customers — in a country of 6.5 million people — and triggering the country’s deepest political crisis in more than a decade.
On Friday evening, President Santiago Peña was impeached after attempting to resign, and his vice president, Pedro Alliana, was sworn in as his replacement.
Authorities quickly arrested Peña, an economist and close ally of US President Donald Trump, and prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility.
Peña has denied wrongdoing and his attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that he was pleading not guilty to the charges.
The scandal has triggered public protests and sharp rebukes from the opposition.
“We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history,” said opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola on Friday. "This impeachment is a first step toward ensuring justice is served."
Manuel Ferreira, a Paraguayan economist and former finance minister, echoed much of the public anger over the case. “This was a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde,” he said. “They didn’t rob us with a pistol, they robbed us with an app. The head of the gang was the president of the republic.”
CENTRAL BANK CHIEF ALSO CHARGED
Until March 2025, Peña had been a business partner of the group that owns ueno. After his election in 2023, he tapped ueno’s former president, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank.
Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier this week. Prosecutors charged him on Saturday with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain. They sought his pretrial detention, which was approved by a judge.
Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment. It was not immediately clear if he had entered a plea in the case.
Peña’s lawyer, Preda, objected to the impeachment, saying that ousting a president during a bank resolution could itself be destabilizing.
“What sets a serious country apart is not that its banks don’t fail, but how it responds,” Preda said on Friday. “If there is one thing that undermines confidence in the financial system, it is attempting to oust the president without evidence.”
Ueno was launched in 2021 as a sleek, millennial-friendly banking app that quickly won over Paraguayans who had been underserved by brick-and-mortar institutions.
It soon became deeply embedded in Paraguay’s payments system. It paired its digital offering with physical branches, later sponsoring sports teams, businesses and events. As of June, public institutions — including Paraguay’s state pension fund — held roughly $850 million in accounts with the bank.
But in recent months, internal regulatory reports warning of excessive lending to certain companies were leaked to local media outlets ABC and Última Hora, triggering political scrutiny of the bank’s lending practices.
Following growing public pressure, Paraguay’s central bank on Tuesday put ueno into resolution — its strongest measure short of immediate liquidation — after determining that ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements, locking millions of customers temporarily out of their accounts.
The central bank said on Saturday that the equivalent of $160 million had since been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the state deposit guarantee scheme.
Authorities have promised that depositors will be reimbursed and say the crisis is confined to ueno. But analysts say the damage to Paraguay’s reputation as a stable investment destination in South America may linger far longer than the bank resolution itself.
“This is the moment when Paraguay must demonstrate that its institutions are functioning,” Ferreira said.

title: Trump thinks he will meet Xi and Putin at China APEC summit
full_text:
Nov 8 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Sunday he thinks he will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders’ summit in China next week and discuss ending the war in Iran and denuclearization.
Trump told reporters before flying back to Washington from Florida that he will travel to China for the APEC summit, set for November 18-19 in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
"One of the meetings, I think, will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that’ll be interesting. We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we’ll be talking a lot of things. We’re trying to end the war in Iran," he said.
Trump said in October that he was open to three-way arms control talks with Xi and Putin, which he said would focus on denuclearization.
The Wall Street Journal later reported that Putin has pitched using a trilateral meeting to discuss an end to Russia’s long-running war in Ukraine.
Trump said in an interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes program that "I believe we’re very close to making a deal" to end the Russia-Ukraine war that would result in a "little bit different shape Ukraine," without offering specifics.
